rationale: The strongest CRC signal in stool is a set of oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella). Each one is sparse and found in only some patients, so a random forest splitting on single genera picks up the signal unevenly. I'm adding two features built from taxonomy names: the summed log-abundance of these genera and how many of them are present. These pool the weak, scattered signals into one stable feature and should also carry over to other CRC studies.

Most of the ~hundreds of genera in Baxter's data are rare. Each one shows up in only a few samples, so it adds noise that the random forest wastes splits on, both in the random feature subsets and the depth-unlimited trees. This change drops any genus found in fewer than 5% of the training-fold samples, before training. The 5% cutoff should still keep the sparse but recurrent CRC markers like Fusobacterium and Parvimonas. The filter is label-free and built from taxonomy names, so it should carry over to the other CRC studies.

Right now every OTU without a genus assignment gets lumped into one "g__" bucket. That throws a large share of reads from different families into a single meaningless feature; many Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae and Enterobacteriaceae OTUs are unclassified at genus level. I'll label each unclassified OTU by its deepest named rank (e.g. "f__Lachnospiraceae;g__") and add family-level totals next to the genera. That keeps the family-level shifts linked to CRC, and since it uses only taxonomy names it should still carry over to other studies.

The random forest reads each genus on its own and cuts on raw relative abundances, so it can't easily pick up the coordinated multiplicative shifts that make up CRC dysbiosis, such as oral pathobionts rising while butyrate producers fall. I'll add a second model: an L2 logistic regression on centered log-ratio (CLR) transformed genus abundances, with the regularization strength chosen by inner CV on the training fold. Its predictions are rank-averaged with the random forest's. The two models make different errors, and both are built from taxonomy names, so the combination should also carry over to the other CRC studies.

CRC stool tends to lose overall diversity, a whole-community shift that a model working one genus at a time can't express. I'm adding depth-robust alpha-diversity features computed from OTU counts: Shannon, inverse Simpson, and expected richness at a fixed depth of 1000 reads, calculated analytically so no random subsampling is needed. They go to both the random forest and, standardized, to the CLR logistic regression. These features don't depend on OTU ids or taxonomy names, so they should carry over to the other CRC studies.

The strongest CRC markers in stool (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) carry their signal mostly through whether they are detected at all, not how abundant they are. The CLR model's tiny pseudocount mixes that detection signal with abundance noise. This adds a third ensemble member, an L2 logistic regression on genus presence/absence with C tuned by inner CV, rank-averaged with the existing random forest and CLR models, to give the ensemble a less-correlated, detection-based view that is also less sensitive to differences in sequencing depth between studies.

The CLR model currently gives every zero the same pseudocount (1e-5 relative abundance), but a zero only means the genus was below the detection limit, and that limit depends on how deeply the sample was sequenced. I'm switching to a count-based pseudocount, log((count+0.5)/depth), so zeros in shallow and deep samples get pseudo-abundances that match their actual detection limits. This should cut the depth-driven noise in the CLR features and in the geometric-mean centering, and it should make the model sturdier on other studies with different sequencing depths. The random forest inputs are unchanged.

Pure L2 spreads the logistic weights over 100+ mostly noisy CLR genera, but the CRC signal sits in a handful of oral pathobionts that rise together and a few butyrate producers that fall. This change switches the CLR logistic regression to an elastic net, with the L1 ratio (0 to 0.75) and C chosen jointly by grouped inner CV on the training fold, so the model can shrink uninformative genera to zero. Including 0 in the ratio grid lets inner CV fall back to plain L2 if sparsity doesn't help.

The random forest still runs on sklearn defaults: about √p (~11) genera tried per split and leaves fully grown down to one sample. With ~230 training samples and a CRC signal concentrated in a few sparse genera, both defaults may be wrong: the markers rarely get offered at a split, and single-sample leaves give noisy probabilities that hurt ranking. This change picks `max_features` (√p, 0.2 or 0.33) and `min_samples_leaf` (1, 3 or 5) by out-of-bag AUROC within the training fold, so it uses training labels only and needs no extra refit.

The L2 logistic regression now also gets the CLR of family-level totals, alongside the genus-level CLR. Many CRC-linked shifts happen across whole families, and family features let genera in the same family pool their weak signals, which the genus-only L2 penalty cannot do. The random forest inputs stay exactly the same; last time, family features hurt when they went into the forest together with a new labelling of unclassified OTUs.

I'm adding a third model to the rank average: a shallow CatBoost model trained on the CLR genus features. Fixed, conservative settings (depth 4, slow learning rate, ordered boosting) hold down overfitting at about 230 training samples. Trees split on CLR values, which measure each genus against the sample's geometric mean rather than its raw share. So this model can catch threshold and interaction effects (oral pathobiont blooms together with butyrate-producer loss) that the linear CLR model can't, while making different errors from the random forest on raw relative abundances.

The CLR centre is currently the mean log-abundance over all ~150 filtered genera. Most of them are often zero and get the pseudocount, so how many zeros a sample has (a mix of richness and sequencing depth) shifts every CLR feature together and blurs the log-ratio signal. I'm switching the reference to the geometric mean of "core" genera, those detected in at least 80% of training-fold samples, which are almost never zero. Each feature becomes a cleaner log-ratio of a genus against a stable set of common gut genera, used by both the logistic regression and CatBoost. The core set is picked by name and without labels, so it carries over across studies.

With only about 230 training samples, a single CatBoost run with `rsm=0.5` depends heavily on its random seed: some runs rarely offer the sparse CRC markers (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas and similar) in early trees, which makes its test ranking noisy. This change averages five CatBoost runs with different seeds. Nothing else changes, so the boosting member's variance should drop and the rank-averaged ensemble should get steadier, without making the model more complex or adding study-specific features.

I'm adding two compositional "balance" features to the log-ratio inputs of the logistic regression and CatBoost (the random forest is unchanged). The first is the geometric-mean log-abundance of the oral pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas, Peptostreptococcus, Porphyromonas, Gemella) relative to the core-genus reference. The second is the log-ratio of those pathobionts against the butyrate producers (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Butyricicoccus, Anaerostipes, Coprococcus). Round 1 gave the forest raw summed abundances. These are instead log-ratio balances that pool the sparse CRC-raised markers and contrast them with the genera CRC depletes. They are built from taxonomy names only, so they should carry over to the other CRC studies.

I'm adding a fourth member to the rank average: an ExtraTrees model trained on the core-reference log-ratio genera. ExtraTrees picks its split thresholds at random, which gives a smoother, lower-variance ranking than the RF on raw abundances or the boosted trees, and that suits about 230 training samples with sparse, threshold-like markers such as the oral pathobionts. Adding a decorrelated member helped before in round 11.

CatBoost can only split on one genus at a time, so it struggles with community-wide gradients that are linear combinations of many genera, such as enterotype axes or a dysbiosis axis. CRC stool shifts along exactly these broad directions. This change adds the top 10 principal coordinates of the standardized core-reference log-ratio genera to CatBoost's inputs only. The PCA is fit without labels on the training fold. This gives the boosted trees an Aitchison-geometry ordination view, which the ensemble has not used yet, while the RF and logistic-regression members stay exactly as they are.

For the log-ratio logistic regression, the sparse genera kept by the 5% filter are mostly zeros replaced by the pseudocount. After standardization, each becomes a mostly arbitrary zero-vs-nonzero feature that the L2 penalty must weigh equally with the denser, more informative genera. So this change lets grouped inner CV on the training fold choose that model's prevalence cutoff from {5%, 10%, 20%}, together with C. The RF, CatBoost and the core reference set stay unchanged, and the filter is still label-free and based on taxonomy names.

Every genus currently gets the same pseudocount (1e-5) before the log-ratio. For genera that are usually abundant, a zero then lands several log units below their smallest observed value, which makes it an extreme outlier that drives the standardized L2 logistic regression. I'm switching to a per-genus pseudocount of half that genus's smallest nonzero relative abundance in the training fold. The pseudocount is label-free and keyed by taxonomy name, so zeros sit just below each genus's own detection floor. Sparse markers like Fusobacterium keep a pseudocount close to the current one, so their presence signal stays.

The logistic regression currently z-scores every log-ratio genus. That inflates near-constant ratios among the common core genera to the same scale as the large, informative changes in the sparse CRC pathobionts (Fusobacterium, Parvimonas and similar). This change keeps the natural log-ratio units instead: each genus is centred, then all genera are divided by one shared scale factor. The L2 penalty then treats a given fold-change the same for every genus, and inner CV picks C over a slightly wider grid.

Right now the three members are rank-averaged with equal weights, even though they probably differ in strength. My guess is the log-ratio models are stronger than the RF on raw abundances. This change re-runs the whole three-model pipeline inside grouped inner CV on the training fold, picks blend weights on a coarse grid by mean inner-fold AUROC, and then shrinks them halfway back toward equal weights. Shrinking limits overfitting with only about 230 training samples.
